speechtext:
The house resumed, from Monday, May 30, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-178, respecting the organization of the government of Canada and matters related or incidental thereto-Mr. Pearson-Mr. Batten in the chair.
On clause 29-duties, powers and functions of the minister.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
When the committee rose on Monday, clause 29 of the bill was being considered.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at this stage of our consideration of the bill we are dealing with a department which will have as its responsibility perhaps the most vital area for Canada's future, namely, the responsibility on the one hand for developing and co-ordinating policies, plans and programs with respect to Canada's resources in co-operation with the provinces, plans for the development of the resources of the territories, the territorial waters and the continental shelf under the jurisdiction of the federal government on the other hand, and bringing those plans into a

co-ordinated whole, thereby giving to this country one of the surest and most important springboards or foundations to ensure the maintenance of our independence, our future prosperity, our growth and survival as a nation, as well as the ability to play an ever more important part in the community of nations.
It is in this context that I want to discuss the deficiencies of the plans and of the organization proposed for this department. I regret that the minister who is designated as minister of this department is not in the committee at the moment because it would be interesting, and I believe important, to have his explanations at this stage and his answers with respect to our criticisms, not of the expressed intent of the legislation but rather of the ways in which it falls short of implementing that intent.
Last evening, Mr. Chairman, I had just finished pointing out the inconsistencies between policy in connection with this new department as stated by the Prime Minister on various occasions and the implementation of that policy as reflected in the right hon. gentleman's speech on second reading.
Let me review the situation very briefly, Mr. Chairman. The object on the government side, as stated by the Prime Minister and others, is to consolidate the responsibility for the development of resources policy. Unfortunately the accomplishment so far as this bill is concerned is a complete division of responsibility in that field between two departments. Indeed, in my submission, never was a policy so good in principle so completely defeated in detail by the results of legislation introduced ostensibly to implement that policy.
Last night I had directed attention to the statement of the Prime Minister which is reported at page 5431 of Hansard as to the roles and responsibilities of the two ministers concerned, the minister of Indian affairs and northern development on the one hand and the minister of energy, mines and resources on the other, and I had pointed out the areas of potential conflict.
This process of outlining conflict and division was continued in the speech of the Prime Minister in the tortured explanation he gave, as reported on the balance of page 5431 and down through the first column of page 5432 of Hansard, including his very inept use of the words "dry land" and "wet land". Well, Mr. Chairman, perhaps his use of those words is not so inept after all; they may be a pretty
May 31, 1966

apt description of the state of the government administration as it will exist after this bill goes through.
Wet land, as I appreciate it, Mr. Chairman, is usually a bog, and if not drained it becomes a quicksand. I have a very acute suspicion that the future course of administration in this field, if this legislation goes through in its present form, will be bogged down in the wet land left by the Prime Minister's proposals and it will need more than the ordinary lifebuoy to drag it out of the quicksand in which it will founder.
I want to direct the committee's attention to the specific passages found at the bottom of the first column on page 5432 and the top of the second column where the Prime Minister is reported as follows:
To avoid confusion the minister of energy, mines and resources will handle the administrative work for the islands in Hudson bay, Hudson strait and Ungava bay, as well as for the underwater areas south of a certain line.
In other words, as a purely pragmatic administrative arrangement, the water areas have been placed with the land jurisdiction in the Arctic archipelago where the land is the most extensive and important element, and the land areas have been placed with the water in the Hudson Bay area where the water areas are very much larger than that of the islands. The dividing line, so far as the departments are concerned, will run substantially along the south coast of Southampton and Baffin Islands.
So, Mr. Chairman, we have one of the most important areas of jurisdiction in resource planning and development divided in half arbitrarily.
Then the Prime Minister, failing so utterly to appreciate the disastrous consequences of that division, went on to say:
This division is not reflected in the present bill because it has no legal consequences or significance.
What an abysmal failure, Mr. Chairman, to appreciate the very far reaching significance of what is proposed. The Prime Minister dismisses it in his next words:
It is simply a division of federal administrative responsibility between two federal ministers about which I thought I should inform the house.
I wish indeed that we could take it as casually as does the Prime Minister. It indicates a complete lack of awareness on the part of the government of any of the significance of this field of resource development, and with the tremendous potential in the northern areas and in the continental shelf it especially indicates a complete unawareness of the importance of co-ordinating policies in
Government Organization this regard. Here we have the most confusing division with respect to administrative arrangements. Did you ever hear of such a half-baked idea of dividing administrative responsibility for areas having the same general problems between two different ministers?
Perhaps even more important, Mr. Chairman, than the chaos created by this administrative division is the fact that the bill is completely silent as to the responsibility for planning and co-ordination of programs for development. It is important that we bear in mind this distinction between responsibility for administration and carrying out plans and physical development on the one hand and the responsibility for making those plans and co-ordinating national policy on the other.
The bill having created chaos by an administrative division, Mr. Chairman, it further confuses the situation by being silent as to the responsibility for planning within the area of the continental shelf. I say that because in clause 17 the minister of Indian affairs and northern development is given responsibility for the territories and their resources and affairs; and while I may have some reservations about the effect of the wording, nevertheless in so far as administrative responsibility is concerned on the whole I think that is sound. As the Prime Minister has pointed out, the minister is in effect acting as trustee for future provinces. This, of course, is acceptable, and in that respect I am sure the territories will co-operate with the minister of energy, mines and resources with respect to the planning and co-ordination of programs in those areas.
However, Mr. Chairman, although the minister of northern development is given responsibility for the territories and their resources and affairs, nowhere is anyone given responsibility for the resources underlying the territorial waters of Canada or the resources of the continental shelf, that is to say, responsibility for the planning, programming and co-ordination of the development programs. In clause 29, the clause now under consideration, no mention is made of these areas or their resources.
Our view is that there must be the clearest definition of administrative responsibility and responsibility for planning and development of resource policy in these areas which, as I have said, constitute a large part of one of the most vital areas of Canadian development and interest. In our view, Mr. Chairman, you simply cannot leave out responsibility for
May 31. 1966

Government Organization planning in one half the area of Canada-the territories, the territorial waters and the continental shelf.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
We therefore propose to move two amendments to rectify this situation. The first would be an amendment to give to the minister of energy, mines and resources responsibility for the administration of the resources underlying the territorial waters within the continental shelf in so far as these belong to Canada. This amendment and its results must be read to some extent, of course as subject to whatever ruling the Supreme Court of Canada may make with respect to jurisdiction in this field.
I pause here, Mr. Chairman, to say that in our view, as we have already expressed it, if the ruling should support the position taken by the government of Canada there must be immediately a discussion with the provinces with regard to a fair apportionment of the benefits of these resources.
The second amendment we will move is an amendment having as its purpose to make clear that the minister has responsibility for planning and co-ordinating programs for all of these resources. Both of these amendments refer to clause 29 of the bill. I say this because I should like to complete my remarks and then speak only briefly before moving the second amendment. We feel that there must be an amendment to make sure that this minister has responsibility for planning and co-ordinating the programs for resources. So far as national responsibility is concerned for co-ordinating these plans and programs, we feel there is at the moment a substantial gap which is not repaired by the inclusion in clause 31 of the bill of the proposed new section 8A of the Resources and Technical Surveys Act.
It should be borne in mind that although there is presently in the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources Act section 7 which clearly delineates the responsibility and authority of the minister for planning in this regard, that section is being repealed. In our view nothing adequate is provided to take its place.
When I move the second amendment I shall go into a little more detail as to why we feel the proposed section 8A of the Resources and Technical Surveys Act is not adequate to fill this gap. I mention the proposed amendment now because I want the committee to realize that the two amendments are complementary. The first one,

which I will move in a moment, is to make it clear that the minister has responsibility for administration of the resources of the territorial waters and continental shelf instead of that responsibility being bifurcated as at present.
The second amendment would give the minister of energy, mines and resources responsibility and authority for planning, so far as the federal government is concerned, in this area and of co-ordinating these plans between the federal and provincial authorities. On that basis, Mr. Chairman, I move:
That Section 29 of the Bill be amended by deleting the word "and" at the end of subclause (b) and adding thereto the following subclauses:
(d)	the resources underlying the territorial waters of Canada: and
(e)	the resources underlying the continental shelf in so far as the same are assigned to Canada by the international agreement respecting the continental shelf reached at Geneva in 1958.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: Is the committee ready for the question?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak to this amendment and say a few words in response to the points brought forward by the hon. member for Kamloops. He told us that a committee of his party had canvassed the situation and decided it was imperative that the resources of Canada, their organization and planning for their exploitation should be held in one department and not more than one. I am quite certain that does not represent the viewpoint of all the members of his own party. The hon. member referred to the regrettable gap that existed, and I think there is a gap in his knowledge of the particular conditions that exist in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. I am going to tell him now that no member of a government who had allocated to him the responsibility for the development of Northwest Territories and the Yukon could discharge that responsibility or have any hope of discharging it unless he had control of the resources of these particular areas.
The other day the Prime Minister referred to the minister charged with this responsibility. I am quite certain that these views I am now giving to the hon. member for Kamloops would be corroborated by the former ministers in his party who have had the responsibility that I now have. The first impression one gets when one goes to the Northwest Territories, and to a lesser extent the Yukon, is that there are no resources above the ground. There has been a long-held hope that there are great resources under the ground. I
May 31. 1966

need only remind the house again, to prove that this is the very fortunate case, that in one year from 1964 to 1965, as a result of the building of the Pine Point Railway, the production of metals in the Northwest Territories rose from $17 million to $74 million. In the current year it is going to exceed $100 million. I predict it will go on to many hundreds of millions of dollars because of the development that is taking place there.
The people who reside there are hopeful of creating something other than the type of government they enjoy at the present time. They can look forward to the development of what the Prime Minister referred to hopefully the other day as one or more provinces in an area where the resources are conserved and developed for their advantage.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
In order to improve the living standards of the Eskimo and Indian people in the north it is necessary to relate these native people to the resources which lie there. The hon. member has made an unconvincing case. I am sure he would not have attempted it in this house had he made a visit to the territories or been in touch with members of his own party who have responsibilities there.
With regard to offshore rights, let me say that we have in Canada at the present time about 1,400,000 cubic miles of sedimentary rock. Not all sedimentary rock contains oil but all oil comes from sedimentary rock.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
More than one million cubic miles of this rock is in the high Arctic islands entirely apart from the Northwest Territories compared with 135,000 cubic miles to be found in Alberta which is today our great source of oil.
So we are extremely enthusiastic about the development of the north and I as minister have to relate the ambitions, the hopes and the plans of the people who live there to conditions as they exist today. The population in the north wishes its resources to be maintained in order that the people may be able to develop the type of government they want. It will therefore be necessary to refuse to accept this amendment at this time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
The minister has rejected the amendment and advanced an argument in support of its rejection apparently without having read the terms of the proposal. I cannot believe that a colleague of mine in this house from British Columbia would be so

Government Organization incapable of understanding an amendment unless he had failed to read it. I can only suppose that he did not read it and that he is stubbornly determined to oppose it simply because it comes forward as a constructive suggestion from the official opposition.
I was glad to find the hon. gentleman paying tribute to the work started by the Conservative government in connection with the Pine Point Railway. It is unusual to find members opposite saying anything good about the government which preceded their own.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: There is little that can be said.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
Had the minister paused to reflect he would have realized that members of a government which took such an interest in developing the north would scarcely fail to recognize the importance of developing the administrative integrity of the resources in that area.
I should also like to inform the minister, in order to keep the record straight, that I visited the territories on two occasions during the time I had some responsibility in that area in connection with the R.C.M.P. and the administration of justice. I took advantage of that opportunity to talk to the people there and became acquainted with their ambitions and their views. I realize how important it is to the development of their plans that we should maintain the administrative integrity of those resources in the area. I should also like to assure the minister that I have discussed this question with my hon. friends in this party including, of course, the hon. member for Yukon. Unlike the situation in the hon. gentleman's own party, there is no internal dissension within our ranks.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
We are not divided by the kind of dissension which makes it impossible for members of the government opposite to introduce some of their most important pieces of legislation, the kind of dissension which holds up the Bank Act.
I have indeed discussed this question with my hon. friends of this party including the hon. member for Yukon. The essential point, and one which the minister has failed to appreciate, is that the amendment I have presented in no way lessens the administrative responsibility of the minister of Indian affairs and northern development in relation to resources within the territories. It changes in no way the provisions of section 17 of the
May 31, 1966

Government Organization bill. What it does is to straighten out the bifurcated responsibility for the administration of the shelf and of the territorial waters, that is the resources of the shelf outside the land areas of the territories. Whatever the minister may say, this is a desirable and, indeed, an essential development if we are to have a policy of co-ordinated resource development in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: would the hon. member permit a question before he resumes his seat? Is he saying that the hon. member for Yukon supports this amendment?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: Most certainly. And let the minister not pretend that this amendment does what he pretends it is doing. I know perfectly well the game the minister is playing. Let him not pretend that this takes away any degree of ministerial responsibility for the administration of the resources within the land area of the territories. It does not.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, having listened to remarks made by the minister I think I should say a few words. As my hon. friend from Kamloops has pointed out, this amendment was put forward in an attempt to rectify what is in our view a schizophrenic act by the government. The Prime Minister, speaking on second reading, announced that the continental shelf would be divided between two ministers. The effect of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Kamloops is to place the shelf under one minister's jurisdiction.
Speaking on second reading I emphasized that in the future the continental shelf would be the subject of hard bargaining with nations like Russia in the west and north and with the countries of Europe to the east while the boundary line was being defined. What struck me as being schizophrenic was that the Prime Minister said that one minister would have responsibility for the shelf north of an arbitrary line while another would have responsibility south of that line. It is my firm belief that responsibility for dealing with foreign powers and for developing policy with respect to the continental shelf should be under one minister.
Had the government been content to leave the whole of the responsibility with the minister of northern affairs there would, I am sure, have been less objection taken here. This is the position adopted by the hon. member for Yukon. He was trying to preserve the resources of this area under the

control of the northern development section of the government. Administratively we want to strengthen the minister of northern affairs. But since there is to be a division of responsibility between the two ministers, then at least let us put responsibility for the continental shelf under one or the other.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
This could be done without reducing the power of the minister one iota under his part of the bill because there is nothing in that part which precisely implies that the continental shelf will be under his department. We simply had a statement by the Prime Minister on second reading, and under the Transfer of Duties Act it can be placed anywhere without statutory enactment.
What we are trying to do by this amendment is to put into clear, statutory language the fact that we want one minister to have charge of the continental shelf. The continental shelf is in two parts, the territorial section which runs from high water mark to three miles offshore and, second, that part of the bottom of the sea which is beyond the three mile limit and extends halfway across the Arctic, the Atlantic and the Pacific, as far as our jurisdiction will go when these areas are finally divided. What we are trying to do is give constructive help to the government so that there will be one minister to whom we can address questions about the behaviour of the government on continental shelf policy.
That is the essence of our amendment. If any one minister had this responsibility I think that would be satisfactory to most of us. As I pointed out on second reading, I thought from the words of the Prime Minister that the workings of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources were being cut down to a provincial government type operation and I stated that I was a little bit frightened about the personality who was going to look after the other department which the Prime Minister called "national". To keep the legislation itself coherent and logical I suggest that these amendments make sense. There is another matter I intend to raise but I think it will come up more properly after a vote is taken on this amendment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had intended to speak earlier but I think my remarks will apply equally well to the amendment and to the bill. I have gone back to the statement made by the Prime Minister on second reading at the pages referred to by the hon. member for Kamloops. It concerns
May 31, 1986
me a bit to see statements that at some time in the future we will have one or more provinces in the north, because there are some Canadians who do not look favourably on the idea of having an additional province in an area of small population, with a complete provincial assembly and all the trappings and expense that go with it in order to administer the affairs of a small group of people.
We seem to have set our minds so firmly on the concept of Canada continuing to proliferate in provinces that we have ignored, until it is almost too late to do anything else, the possibility of other arrangements such as expanding existing provinces and thus negating the necessity of setting up others that will be a material drain on the rest of Canada.
I am concerned that this particular aspect of government reorganization has been introduced at this time and that we are engaging in setting up a department of energy at a time when the question of the territorial shelf and offshore mineral rights has been placed before the Supreme Court of Canada by the federal government. My attention was drawn to a significant editorial in the Toronto Star of yesterday, May 30, under the heading "Stand Up and Lead, Mr. Pepin''. Here is how this distinguished journalist points up the problem:
Mr. Pearson's original idea, evidently, was that Mr. Pepin would be concerned with matters national in character and not relating to any particular province or territory. He seems to have thought at one point that Mr. Laing might function as a "dry land" and Mr. Pepin as a "wet land" minister. These lands underneath the sea are not provincial. Let that be clear. By international law the lands under the sea have been given to Canada, not to any province. Let us be clear about that. This does not mean that the federal government has to administer every little detail, because I am sure there will be discussions with the provinces and the territories about administration. But as to the silly argument that half the wealth of the north is under the sea, that is not the point at all.
Either the minister is to be, as the Prime Minister said, like a provincial minister or he is not. Either the other minister is to be, as the Prime Minister said, a national minister or he is not. The words of the Prime Minister are so clear, Mr. Chairman, that to try to divide a national responsibility and give part of it to a provincial minister just does not make sense.
We are not giving up one bit of the rights of the province of the future in the north to administer its own resources. They go to the high water mark like those of every other province do. The boundary of the province of Ontario stops short of the high water mark. The boundary of the province of Manitoba stops short of the high water mark. The boundary of the province of Quebec stops at the same point, short of the high water mark. Therefore, why should the Northwest Territories have more than any other province? If we are to be consistent, let us keep this bill consistent. If we are to have a national minister, then give him national responsibilities. But do not divide the cake in half.

If we still want to keep the resources of the continental shelf under the jurisdiction of one minister and if it is clearly understood that the continental shelf is to be looked after by the national minister and that the responsibility is delegated to the minister of the north, then that is good enough for me. I am simply making it very clear that a resource which is the property of Canada by the international law of the sea should be dealt with by the national minister.
If parliament wishes to place that national duty upon another minister then that is its privilege. But it should be one or the other, Mr. Chairman. We want that resource dealt with as one unit, as the property of the people of Canada, regardless of negotiations with the provinces or territories in connection with administering it. We will fight hard to keep the power of administration in the hands of the territories so far as administering those resources is concerned, but let me make it very clear that the resources at the bottom of the sea, whether in territorial waters or beyond the territorial waters, are the property of the national government by international law.

This arrangement will not work satisfactorily or efficiently. I believe the time will come in Canada when the administration of mineral development, whether on the land or in territorial waters, will be under the same authority. I believe that it has to come. Mr. Chairman, I should like to make some comments in connection with the amendment we are now considering. I believe it essent.al that the department to be set up should give leadership in the development of our water resources and in the war against pollution. In order to achieve this result it must be given the tools with which to do the job. The minister must be able to give the necessary leadership. We need to look at the proposed set-up in order to decide whether this can be done under the terms of clauses 29, 30 and 31. I will direct my remarks to clause 31 which deals with the authority granted to the minister of energy, mines and resources.
While research, co-ordination and inventory with relation to water resources are a necessary prerequisite to action, it is obvious that action must follow if any leadership is to be given on a national basis. I have, therefore, read and reread the proposed new subsection 8A of the Resources and Technical Surveys Act to determine the real intention of the government in this respect. The foundation for any real action is lacking. May I illustrate my point by an example.
Senior levels of government can best give guidance by the initiation of pilot projects. In the case of the United Nations agencies, the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the International Development Association, pilot projects are undertaken in developing countries to indicate the essential worth of an agricultural, industrial or educational project. The actual development of such projects and the subsequent 23033-3661
Government Organization operation of them are strictly within the field of the developing nation itself. The pilot project, however, is financed by the international agency to give leadership and impetus to the commencement of such projects.
Likewise, in the fields of water resources and pollution pilot projects are essential. In the Ruhr valley of Germany water resource co-operative associations have been operating since the year 1904. Whole river basins are controlled by one authority and the cost of pollution control is charged directly to those who pollute the stream in proportion to the extent of pollution. The system has been successful in spite of the fact that the Ruhr valley is one of the most highly industrialized and heavily populated areas of the world.
These associations were given almost complete multipurpose authority over water quantity and quality in entire watersheds by their special laws. They have for up to 50 years made comprehensive plans for waste disposal, water supply, flood control and land drainage. Members of the association are principally the municipal administrative districts and the industrial enterprises, and general public supervision is carried out by a government ministry. They have authority to plan and construct facilities for water resources management and to assist their members with the cost of constructing and operating such facilities.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
On February 23, 1966, giving acknowledgement of the need for federal leadership in the urgent problems of pollution control in the United States, President Johnson sent a message to Congress proposing the setting up of pollution control programs for entire river basins. He proposed combined efforts by all means at American disposal, federal, state, local and private, to reduce progressively the pollution of United States waters. He proposed a clean rivers demonstration program which would unite all the pollution control activities in a single river basin from its source to its termination. I have complete details of his proposals and of the federal participation, but they are not essential to the point I am trying to make.
To turn now to Canada's problems, the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys seems to be saying in his speeches that the management of water resources and pollution control are a provincial responsibility. He seems to be saying that the federal government should not evolve a national water
576G
May 31. 1966

Government Organization resources policy or program or a national anti-pollution drive. He seems to feel that he does not have either the constitutional authority or the responsibility for a national program involving water resources.
According to a press report of a speech he made in Toronto on Friday, May 27, he outlined the federal government role in water policy as one of taking inventory, of basic and applied research, of development of nationally accepted pollution guide lines and of continuing liaison with the provinces and the United States. These are all necessary prerequisites to a policy of action on water resources and pollution, but they are not enough. They do not provide for any action by the federal government. They provide no leadership.
The Ontario Water Resources Commission is doing an excellent job in pollution control and so are many other provincial bodies. But the development of industry, increased population and new types of waste are making the race against pollution a losing one for all local jurisdictions. Furthermore, we must make plans for the future and carry them out on a national basis.
A pilot project for a clean water development involving federal, provincial, municipal and industrial co-operation could well be carried out in several areas of Canada. Indeed, we do not need to go very far for the essentials of such a project because one could well be carried out on the Ottawa river. There is a twofold federal interest. First, the river forms a boundary between two provinces and, second, the river flows through the national capital region. There are also strong provincial interests.
On the Ontario side there are two conservation authorities in existence, one on the South Nation river and the other on the Rideau, the latter having recently been formed. However, there is no authority for the Ottawa valley as such and it would be useless to have such an authority on one side of the river if there were not a similar authority on the other. There are extensive municipal and industrial interests because each municipality and industry is interested in receiving clean water from upstream. This is a pilot project in which the federal government could well give leadership. I mention it only as an example but it is a fair example. It is nearby, and the proposal indicates that the federal government can easily undertake leadership in a pilot project.

While we have reasonably good working arrangements for international boundary waters under the International Joint Commission, it is very strange that we have no procedures established for dealing between and among provinces on water resources and pollution. Surely this is a fundamental federal responsibility. Surely this should be a first priority for the new department which we are considering.
We hear a great deal of talk about constitutional problems. These are always present in a federal system such as we have, but while they are present they have not deterred the federal government from taking leadership and responsibility in the purely provincial matters of health involving hospital insurance and medical care, of welfare involving pensions, of education involving university grants and vocational schools. Why then do we tread so timidly in dealing with the urgent national problem of pollution?
Returning again to the powers proposed to be given to the new department under the amendment, I believe that this amendment is necessary in order to give the minister authority to deal with the problems that are facing us. I can find no clear wording in the bill as it stands which indicates an intention to propose and carry out pilot projects under federal initiative. The very wording of the clause which includes the words "coordinating, promoting and recommending" but not the words "carrying out", or anything similar to them, indicates the lack of resolution of the government in this field. This is why I rose to speak in connection with this amendment.
I sincerely believe that the problems of water resources and water pollution in Canada are serious and deserve national attention, and to get national attention the leadership must come from the federal government. It is true that there is provincial responsibility. There are indications that the provinces are not only aware of the problem but are doing something about it. I think they are looking to the federal government to take the initiative. I think they are looking for the passage of this bill which to some degree at least will co-ordinate the responsibilities for water resources.
I believe the provinces are waiting for an indication from the federal government that it intends to take the leadership and lay plans for the future. We all know that pollution is not a problem that can be settled quickly but a start on settling it can be made
May 31, 1966

quickly. Pilot projects can be commenced. Policies can be laid down and a start can be made with leadership from the federal government and from the new minister. It is essential that this be done, but what is completely lacking in this bill is any indication that the government intends to give the minister that authority. There is also a lack of intention on the part of the minister to take any leadership.
I hope that the amendment will be given serious consideration. If it is not accepted then there will be an acknowledgement by the government that it has no intention to give the minister any power to do anything more than undertake research, to make plans, to put forward proposals and to co-ordinate activities. These are all essential but following them action will be necessary to deal effectively with the problems of pollution.

Mr. Chairman, we must never let that situation arise in Canada. The only way in which we can ensure that it does not arise here is to start now.

the conservation, development and use of the resources of Canada."
If the purpose is to grant to the federal government, by means of a clause in this bill, higher or prior authority over that of the provinces in dealing with the formulating of plans for the development of resources in Canada, I am not in favour of that kind of legislation. I think there needs to be a great deal more co-operation and, what is more, more active ways and means must be found of setting programs in action in so far as water pollution is concerned. But there is nowhere in clause 29, the amendment proposed to clause 29, or for that matter in clause 31 dealing with the new section 8A, anything that confines this matter to water resources. If it is to include other resources I think there will be a very serious constitutional problem in this respect. Even if it is only for water resources it seems to me it is the wrong way of granting this superior authority to the federal government.
What I am saying is not intended to take anything away from the desirability of a higher level of co-operation and more active programming and planning. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources mentioned, I believe, that the conference of ministers was meeting in Winnipeg today and agreement had been reached between the prairie provinces and the federal government to co-operate in developing plans and programs for the Nelson River drainage basin. I have no objection to this and in fact I wholeheartedly support it. In so far as paragraphs 3 and 4 of the proposed amendment are concerned, which call for co-operation with the provinces and the calling of conferences and so on, I think they are almost superfluous to the legislation because this is being done by the minister now. The proof of this is to be found in the example stated today. The minister said that agreement has already been reached with the three prairie provinces with respect to draining the enormous Nelson river basin. and conservation of water resources it had better say what it means and not just refer to the resources of Canada.

In so far as Alberta is concerned I think the act was passed in 1930. If we are to try now to supersede that authority by a clause of this bill, I think we will be doing it in the wrong way and will perhaps wind up with something that is undesirable in the long run.

I suggest that the sponsors of bills of this kind should give more consideration to their responsibilities to parliament. Parliament is not an operation similar to a law office where every client is accepted. Perhaps I am wrong in making such a comparison, but I think that members of this house should consider their responsibilities to parliament before accepting the sponsorship of whimsical legislative measures such as are contained in bills of this type.
If one reads the report of the Superintendent of Insurance regarding loan and trust companies he will find that this particular company does not stack up very well, and I suggest that the sponsor should consider his responsibility seriously and not act as a lawyer handling a client's case. If he is prepared to sponsor such a bill he should be prepared to give a complete and thorough explantion of the reasons behind it. In support of my suggestion let me point out that it appears that very few members are willing to sponsor proposals such as the one before us.
The report of the Superintendent of Insurance makes a distinction between various incorporated companies. The company under consideration falls into a particular category because it was originally incorporated by an act of parliament in 1961. speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-170,
Public Service Collective Bargaining respecting employer and employee relations in the public service of Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is the intention of the government, with the co-operation of hon. members, to proceed with second reading of the three bills, C-170, C-181 and C-182, which together would provide for the introduction of collective bargaining into the public service and for a number of other important reforms in the processes of public administration. If it is agreeable to the house, Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by asking hon. members to consider Bill C-170, the proposed Public Service Staff Relations Act. Following second reading of that bill, I would like to proceed to Bill C-181, the proposed Public Service Employment Act, and then to Bill C-182, which contains proposed amendments to the Financial Administration Act.
Hon. members have already approved the establishment of a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons which, it is hoped, will review all three measures and report its views to the house prior to third reading. It is my intention after each bill has been read a second time to propose a motion to provide for referral to this committee, which has been established by the house.
In speaking to Bill C-170, I would like to begin by reviewing very briefly the principal features of the system of collective bargaining for which it would provide.
Under the proposed system, bargaining rights would be available to virtually all public servants except those carrying managerial responsibilities and those serving management in a confidential capacity. It would not be available to employees of crown corporations now covered by the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, to members of the armed forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, or to certain smaller groups for whom it would be difficult or inappropriate to establish terms and conditions of employment by means of collective bargaining.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
The system would be administered by a staff relations board, similar in composition to the labour relations boards that operate in the different jurisdictions across Canada. The board would have the power to define bargaining units and can certify employee organizations as bargaining agents. It would also provide an administrative umbrella for other third party functions, including the arbitration of disputes and the adjudication of grievances.
May 31, 1966

Public Service Collective Bargaining
For a period of about two years, bargaining units in a large part of the public service would be defined in such a way as to correspond with the occupational groups identified in the classification structure now being developed and implemented by the Civil Service Commission. This feature, recommended by the preparatory committee on collective bargaining, is designed to ensure that bargaining rights are extended as quickly as possible, with a minimum of destruction to the ongoing processes of pay determination, and in a manner consistent with the interests of employees and the effective operation of the public service.
For the great bulk of the public service, the interests of the employer in bargaining would be represented by Treasury Board. Provision is made, however, for the designation as separate employers of a number of agencies, such as the National Research Council and the National Film Board, that have traditionally had a significant measure of independence in matters of personnel management. The interests of employees would be represented, of course, by employee organizations able to meet the normal tests for certification as bargaining agents.
Agreements reached would be binding on the parties. Arguments about their interpretation would be subject to mandatory grievances procedures and, ultimately, to independent adjudication.
The dispute settlement provisions in the bill are of great importance. In applying for certification as a bargaining agent, an employee organization would be required to choose one of two dispute settlement options; one providing for recourse to binding arbitration, the other for a procedure requiring reference to a conciliation board and offering, in defined circumstances, to employees other than those deemed necessary in the interests of the safety or security of the public, the right to strike. Each bargaining agent would be bound by the procedure of its choice and would be unable to change its option for a period of three years. The reason for the three-year period is to move through one bargaining period and on to the next before there can be a change in the option of employee representatives.
The arbitration of disputes would be the responsibility of an independent arbitration tribunal. For any one dispute, the tribunal would consist of a permanent chairman and two members drawn from panels of individuals representing generally the interests of

employer and employees. Awards of the tribunal would be final and binding on both sides.
I want to say how pleased I am, Mr. Speaker, with the reception given by the house to the Prime Minister's statement when he moved the resolution. I am likewise pleased to note the support for the underlying principles of the bill that has been expressed outside this house by the principal employee organizations.
A number of points were made during the debate on the resolution on matters affecting the proposed new system of staff relations in the public service. No doubt all of these will be given careful consideration in the joint committee. In the meantime, I would like to comment on one or two of the more important of those comments which were made.
There were warm words of praise for the National Joint Council of the Public Service of Canada. I am happy to associate myself and the other members of the government with the sentiments expressed. For more than two decades the council has served as a focal point of joint consultation in the public service. Its deliberations have led to a steady stream of improvements in conditions of employement and, what is perhaps more important, a steady growth in the maturity of the relationship between representatives of the employer and the employees.
For some months, Mr. Speaker, the National Joint Council has been reviewing its future role in the light of the anticipated introduction of a system of collective bargaining. Recommendations resulting from this review were approved by the council last week and were received in my office a few days ago. The government will wish to consider these recommendations before taking a definite position on the issues involved. I can now say this much, however: The government believes that in the new system there will be need for an institution like the National Joint Council in which representatives of bargaining agents and representatives of the employer can come together and jointly seek solutions to problems that go beyond those of particular bargaining units. Like the preparatory committee on collective bargaining, we believe that, if preserved and nurtured, the traditions associated with the council could be put to good use in the new system.
In the debate on the resolution, a question was also raised about the future role of the Pay Research Bureau. Let me say at once that in my opinion there can be no doubt
May 31, 1966	COMMONS
about the valuable service rendered by the Pay Research Bureau since its creation in 1957, nor about the increased objectivity which its work has brought to the consideration of the remuneration of employees of the public service. I would like to commend officials of the bureau who, in the past dec-cade, have built it into one of the most respected research organizations of its kind in Canada.
As hon. members know, the preparatory committee made quite specific recommendations about the future of the Pay Research Bureau. The government has not yet dealt with these recommendations. It seemed to us that they could not be dealt with in a satisfactory manner until consultations with employee representatives could take place in the full knowledge of the characteristics of the legislation we are now considering. We believe that the Pay Research Bureau should be retained as an independent and impartial unit whose findings are made available to accredited representatives of both employer and employees. We are satisfied, however, that decisions about its future terms of reference and method of operation should be made only after employee representatives have had an opportunity to consider those matters in the context of the collective bargaining legislation and to express to the government their considered views.
In the debate on the resolution, mention was also made of arbitration mechanisms proposed by the preparatory committee, mechanisms which, as the bill indicates, are considered by the government to be appropriate. The arbitration tribunal proposed in the bill is directly comparable to the arbitration tribunal which has successfully dealt with disputes in the Whitley Council system of the United Kingdom since 1925. During the more than 40 years that it has functioned, the British tribunal has dealt with some 600 cases and, throughout this very long period, has enjoyed the confidence and support of representatives of both employees and successive governments.
One hon. member, commenting upon the proposals of the preparatory committee, expressed some doubt as to the wisdom of making no provision for the public expression of dissenting views in awards of the tribunal. It seems to me, however, that an award which associates the chairman of the tribunal with only one of the members is apt to be divisive, encouraging one of the parties to welcome the award and the other to resent it. Public Service Collective Bargaining manner in which awards are to be made is an important element of the proposed legislation that will no doubt be analysed in greater depth in the joint committee. I am sure that members of the committee will wish to ascertain the views of the staff associations on this question. Although our position on this point is by no means rigid, it seems to me at the present time that the proposal for an award signed only by the chairman has much to commend it.
I have already indicated that, where a bargaining agent rejects arbitration in favour of the process involving conciliation and the right to strike, provision is made for the designation of employees whose services are necessary in the interests of the safety and security of the public.
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
This proposal has been the subject of some comment outside the house and it is important, I think, that there should be no misunderstanding of its character and significance. The absolute requirement for such a provision is clear, I think, to anyone who comprehends the many areas where public servants provide services which, if withdrawn in some circumstances, could endanger individuals in the community. A number of examples come to mind, including prison security, air traffic control, and hospital care. The identification of all such services is of course not possible without a systematic review of work being performed throughout the whole public service of Canada.
In considering this aspect of the proposed legislation, hon. members must differentiate between what might be described on the one hand as useful and important services, and on the other, as services necessary in the interests of the safety and security of the public. Almost every public service is, in one way or another, important to the well-being of the community. The proposed limitation on the right to strike is not intended to deny that right to all whose services may be deemed important. Such a limitation would be so severe as to serve almost as a statutory prohibition of all strike action.
In relation to this aspect of the proposed legislation, however, it is not necessary for me to remind hon. members of the ultimate sovereignty of parliament and its authority to protect and safeguard the public interest. It is, I believe, our duty in dealing with issues of this kind to legislate in such a way as to deny no man the ordinary rights and privileges of Canadian citizens unless in the public
5788	COMMONS
Public Service Collective Bargaining interest it is absolutely necessary to do so. On the other hand, no one should doubt the capacity or willingness of parliament to qualify such rights and privileges where they are being used in gross disregard for the well-being of the community.
Let me remind hon. members of the objectives of this legislation which the Prime Minister suggested that all members should bear in mind as they examine and evaluate the provisions of this bill. These were: first, to protect the public interest; second, to respond in an understanding and responsible manner to the aims and aspirations of organized employees; third, to preserve the capacity of the public service to function in an efficient manner; and fourth, to respect the principles underlying industrial relations law and practice in Canada.
With respect to the first objective, there has not been, and indeed there cannot be, any equivocation. The public interest must be served. In the development of all aspects of these bills, this basic requirement has been a primary consideration.
With respect to the second objective, I am satisfied that in its principal elements this legislation is a reasonable response to the claims of all interested employee organizations. However, I do not expect every one of these organizations to support all the details of the bill, if only because their wishes and aspirations are not in all respects the same.
With respect to the third objective, I believe that improvements in morale will result from the introduction of collective bargaining and mandatory grievance procedures, and will in time produce substantial gains in the efficiency of the public service. Hon. members know that this legislation is only one of a number of steps which the government is taking, or proposing to take, to gear the administrative machinery of government to the present and future demands of Canadian society.
Many of these steps are in the field of personnel management. Reforms in this field are as important and as necessary as reforms in the processing of income tax returns-I might perhaps say they are even more important-or as the need for reforms in the presentation of estimates to parliament. Each in its own way represents a change which adapts the machinery of government to the new age in which we live. Each in its own way will, I am sure, contribute to the administrative efficiency of the public service.

Finally, the proposed legislation in most of its basic principles is consistent with the provisions of statute law which regulate these matters in the private sector. It provides for the definition of bargaining units and the certification of bargaining agents. It imposes an obligation on the employer to negotiate in good faith with certified bargaining agents with a view to the conclusion of collective agreements. It provides for third-party adjustment of disputes arising out of the interpretation or application of collective agreements and arbitral awards. It permits employees to choose freely the organizations by which they wish to be represented in collective bargaining, and to replace those organizations when they no longer enjoy their confidence. It prohibits interference in the affairs of employee organizations by representatives of the employer, and it assures the right of every employee to belong to an employee organization of his choice.
In two important respects, Mr. Speaker, the proposed legislation goes beyond that which governs the relationship of employers and employees in most other jurisdictions. It grants bargaining rights to all professional employees, and it provides to all employee organizations applying for certification as bargaining agents the right to choose between alternative methods of dispute settlement.
In the long history of staff relations in the public service of Canada, organized professional employees have played a prominent and responsible part. In recent years they have been among those advocating a system of collective bargaining and arbitration. Now that such a system is being provided, the government can see no reason why they should be denied access to it.
As far as we know, the proposal for alternative methods of dispute settlement has no counterpart in other jurisdictions. We believe however that, when coupled with the provision for the designation of employees necessary to the safety and security of the public, it represents a sensible response to the requirements of the public service. As hon. members know, some groups of organized employees have expressed a strong desire for a system in which disputes are settled by binding arbitration and others have made it clear that they oppose arbitration as a matter of principle. The government has concluded that in the public service, in a system designed to embrace a wide spectrum of occupations-indeed, it will be the largest
May 31, 1966

employer-employee relationship governed by collective bargaining in this country-organized employees should have the freedom to choose a dispute settlement procedure with which they are in basic agreement and by which they are prepared to be bound.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is as complex and intricate as it is voluminous. Together with its companion measures, the Public Service Employment Act and the amendment to the Financial Administration Act, it constitutes an immense change in the approach to personnel management and staff relations in the public service.
At the resolution stage I endeavoured to outline the principles which we on this side think should govern collective bargaining in the public service, and indicated clear support for those principles. With reservations which I shall mention tonight, I support this bill although I must assert that a detailed study of it and of its two companion measures leaves many questions unanswered. The minister's statement tonight, to which I listened carefully, did not remove these uncertainties.
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
It is still not clear how this collective bargaining bill will be integrated with the regular procedures under the new public service employment bill and with financial control under the Financial Administration Act. Indeed, few of these questions have been answered by the minister's opening presentation tonight, and they will require to be pursued before the proposed joint special committee of the Senate and House of Commons.
Because this bill will go to that joint special committee I believe it is desirable, indeed important, that members of this house should not adopt final, or hard and fast positions on second reading. In the special committee all interested parties will have the opportunity to give evidence and make submissions, and thereafter there will be ample time to take up positions.
Within the public service itself, sir, there is still but little appreciation of how radical, indeed how revolutionary will be the changes wrought by this bill. Many of the familiar and established procedures will go out the window and be wholly abandoned. The whole system of salary determination which has been built up over the years will be altered beyond recognition. This will not be achieved
Public Service Collective Bargaining without major headaches-headaches for management and employee alike. There will be major and startling upsets in the public service of this country.
In many departments wholesale dissatisfaction has already arisen with the classification revision program, the so-called red circling program. Many employees feel a sense of discrimination and hurt, and I hope the government will be able to allay those fears which have already been aroused.
The house should not think that the public service is wholly unanimous in favouring the changes now proposed. The old system of salary determination, based upon reports of the Pay Research Bureau and involving cyclical revision, is not unanimously condemned by any means. Many intelligent civil servants would prefer to retain the existing system in preference to collective bargaining. For myself, sir, I believe the change to a system of collective bargaining is both inevitable and desirable and will accrue to the great advantage of the majority of civil servants.
Equally, I have never concealed my hope that it could have been achieved by a process of gradualism. In my view the Whitley councils in Great Britain would be the best model for us. They have no statutory or legislative basis, and my hope had been that before this we could achieve the same results in this country by a process of broadening down from precedent to precedent. It became obvious, of course, that this was not possible, and that section 7 of the old act would not lead to this result.
Obviously we have come to the stage today where we must now have this legislation, but what troubles me most about this bill is its complexity. It purports to dot every "i" and to cross every "t". In the joint special committee I shall need some convincing that this exhaustive complexity will not lead to inflexibility or to excessive rigidity in employee relations. I say to you, sir, nothing could be more undesirable than to initiate a new system of collective bargaining and confine it in a legislative strait-jacket at the very outset.
In my view the new system must have room for experimentation, room to live, to breathe and to grow. Personally, I have never seen any employee relations legislation so exhaustive, so saturated with detail as is this bill. In committee I submit that we must ask ourselves whether this very exhaustiveness is.

Public Service Collective Bargaining not self-defeating-whether the system so rigidly defined may not break down of its own weight. I hope that it will not, but I would like to see less definition, less exhaustive presentation and more opportunity for the system to live and, as I say, to breathe and to grow.
In the final analysis, Mr. Speaker, two human factors will determine the success or failure of the new system-first, the calibre of the persons appointed to the Public Service Staff Relations Board and to the Arbitration Tribunal and, second, the good will and loyal competence of the negotiators for management and the representatives of the bargaining agents. I reiterate what I tried to say a,t the resolution stage, that the appointments to the board and to the tribunal must be of the very highest calibre. There must not be even a breath of suspicion of patronage, and I speak of patronage as either political or bureaucratic. Indeed, sometimes I think bureaucratic patronage is worse than political patronage. I repeat, there must not be the breath of suspicion of patronage in these appointments.
It will be the responsibility of the rank and file of civil servants themselves to make certain that their employee organizations, which will be their bargaining agents, do not fall into improper hands-into power-hungry or influence-seeking cliques. If civil servants generally just leave it to "George", if they let minorities rule the employee organizations, then I say that collective bargaining will be no new Valhalla, and they will have only themselves to blame. The early stages of collective bargaining particularly will necessitate wise leadership and genuine employee relations statesmanship among the heads of the employee organizations.
If I read the bill correctly it does purport to retain as the final basis of an arbitration award the principle of salary determination which has become known as "fair comparison." The government of course should always be a model employer, exercising a good influence towards all employment across the nation, but the role and status of public servants should not get out of line, either upwards or downwards, with those prevailing .generally in similar occupations. The basis of "fair comparison" has worked satisfactorily as a general rule and should be retained as a

statement of what this government is prepared to suggest in respect of the role that the National Joint Council should play.

Fleming, and the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert to establish this bureau. I say to the minister that he must not be at all equivocal on this matter. Now, Mr. Speaker, one of the most important and effective features of this bill is that dealing with grievances. In any organization as large as the public service of this country, the existence of a substantial number of grievances, some well founded some less well founded, is inevitable. At least one quarter of my total working hours each day is devoted to listening to grievances of civil servants in this area and taking them up with ministers or appropriate senior officers. When I sat on the other side of the house, almost two-thirds of my time was devoted to this time consuming but necessary aspect of an Ottawa member's life.
I believe the grievance procedures in this bill are good. Perhaps they will relieve Ottawa area members like my sincere friend from Ottawa East (Mr. Richard) to enable them to devote more time to constructive legislative duties, although I have some doubts. I think my hon. friend from Ottawa East and my hon. friend from Russell (Mr. Tardif) would agree fully with these statements. I know the hon. gentleman who leads this house now, the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) has had more experience than any one of us. One of the ironic things is that civil servants are universally and instinctively against political influence until personal problems arise, and then they

Public Service Collective Bargaining resent it if their M.P. does not have enough pull to fix the problem.
Finally, sir, I should like to deal with the principles of the bill as they affect the right to strike. For myself I want to reserve the right of final decision on the issue until all the evidence has been heard and exhaustive discussion has taken place in the joint special committee. On all sides of the house there are major differences of opinion on this subject. The same is true among the employee organizations.
What I fear is that this bill falls between two stools; it recognizes the right to strike for some employees, but refuses it to others. Then it permits those for whom strike action is recognized to bargain away that right. Frankly, to me, this seems to be an attempt to get on all sides of the issue and is likely to fail for that reason. I have been interested to note that the almost universal reaction of newspaper opinion is firmly against the right to strike. For myself I doubt that either recognition of the right to strike or the prohibition of the right to strike really matters anything like as significantly as some people urge.
Recognition of the right will not make employee organizations any less responsible and, on the other hand, it has been my experience throughout life that prohibitions never have been successful in preventing persons with a sense of moral outrage from taking retaliatory action. Actually the only real issue is not whether a strike can be prevented one way or another, but whether, if held, a strike in the public service would be legal or illegal. However, when you encounter that dread tragedy of a strike of public servants, the question of legality or illegality is not very serious or significant, in my view. It really is only a matter of academic exercise.
Parliament always should be seeking to prevent any conditions arising where the possibility of strike action could ever be contemplated. If, for example, the legitimate grievances of the postal workers as revealed to Judge Anderson and Judge Montpetit had been aired in this chamber, we never would have had a postal strike. Civil servants in the Ottawa area had put all their political eggs in the one Liberal basket at that time, and the Ottawa members were silent. The government just sat on a powder keg until, predictably, it exploded into a postal strike.
Obviously, before third reading, there will be much more to say on this subject of the
May 31, 1966

Public Service Collective Bargaining right to strike. That is all I would wish to say at this particular time. I have made my personal position clear. We should await the hearings and the evidence in the committee before making further comment.
There is one principle of the bill with which the Minister of National Revenue dealt which affects the issue very directly, and which I do not think can be allowed to stand. That is the unique provision that the chairman of an arbitration tribunal shall always be a one-man majority, even when his two colleagues are in disagreement. In committee, this extraordinary principle will have to be eliminated, if arbitration is to be realistic. I never have heard of this type of provision. It may exist elsewhere, but I never have seen a situation where one man can be a majority in a body of three. In committee this extraordinary provision will have to be explained to me in a manner which the minister has not done tonight, or else certainly I will be one of those who decidedly will vote against it.

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) said at the resolution stage when he spoke on behalf of our party, we welcome this legislation. We feel it is an important milestone in the history of the government of this country for us to be establishing the principle of collective bargaining for our federal public servants. We also welcome the other two bills which are companion pieces to this legislation and which will be dealt with after we pass this bill. I refer to the bill establishing the public service employment act and the bill amending the Financial Administration Act.
We welcome the fact that among these pieces of legislation the number of employees who are to be known as public servants is widened, and we welcome the extent to which the government has accepted some of the very useful recommendations of the Glassco Commission. All told, we feel that a good job for the public service and for public servants is being done by bringing forward these three pieces of legislation.
It will be no surprise to any member of this house if I suggest that my speech is not going to be one of nothing but praise. I shall have some criticisms to make. But even so, I wanted my first words to emphasize what has already been said on behalf of this party, namely that we are glad the day has at last come when we are going to establish collective bargaining in the public service. We also welcome the fact that these three pieces of legislation will be referred, after each one has had second reading, to a special committee where we can go into the details of them. I hope the government's attitude will be one that will accept useful and constructive suggestions that are made when these pieces of legislation are before that special committee.
Mr. Speaker, having made it clear that we are pleased to have this legislation, I should like to make a few criticisms and indicate a few points where we think improvements can be made. Necessarily I shall be referring to
May 31, 1966

items that are covered within the contents of the bill, but I shall not break any rule by referring to the clauses as such; rather, I think it is important to do as the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) did, namely give notice at this point of some of the things that we think should be gone into when we have this legislation before the committee.
The first thing I should like to say is that we feel the government at long last having accepted the idea of collective bargaining for public servants, should have demonstrated more confidence in this principle than I believe to be exhibited by the terms of the legislation. I think not only should it have shown more confidence in the principle of collective bargaining, but I agree with the hon. member for Carleton that the government should have shown more confidence in the experience it has had over several decades in dealing with civil servants through their various organizations. Even though it can be said that we are entering a new era, in the sense that we are going to have collective bargaining, it is not the beginning of consultations between the government as employer and its employees.
There has been a good deal of experience in this field. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) tonight paid tribute to the growth and improvement that has taken place in those relations. He referred to the maturity that has come about. It seems to me that if the government does have an awareness of the fact that there has been experience in terms of consultation between the government as employer and its public servants as employees, it should have demonstrated this by not hedging the principle of collective bargaining quite so much as has been done in this piece of legislation.
Part of what I have in mind in this respect was alluded to by the previous speaker when he referred to the complexities of the bill that is now before us. I recognize that it takes a fairly lengthy piece of legislation to deal with this matter, but it does seem to me that those who drafted this bill have gone a little too far in trying to provide for everything. To the extent that an attempt is made by legislation to deal with every possible situation, room for negotiation, room for good will between parties which respect each other is limited.
I suggest that it would be better to rely a little more on the good will and experience that has been built up between the government and its employees. In this connection I

Public Service Collective Bargaining suppose the outstanding example of what I am talking about, when I say there is a lack of confidence in the principle of collective bargaining, is the way in which the government has given the right to strike and at the same time has hedged it. I am aware of the fact that newspaper editorial opinion to a considerable extent has not welcomed the recognition by the government of the right to strike on the part of civil servants, but I should like to commend the government for not having worried about this. I commend it for having accepted the fact that, at least as far as it is prepared to go, civil servants are citizens like the rest of the workers in Canada and should be accorded the same rights.

But when the government gives the right to strike to public servants, and then says that that right can only be exercised if the appropriate bargaining units make a choice in advance to which they are tied for three years, then I submit that it has, to a considerable extent, denied the freedom of the right to strike which has supposedly been given to our civil servants. I am surprised that once the government was prepared to grant the right to strike it did not give it in at least the same and unconditional way that is provided for other employees in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. This requirement that a bargaining unit must decide in advance whether it wants to have recourse to arbitration or whether it wants to retain the right to strike, I suggest is unrealistic and a denial of the right that is supposedly being accorded.
Not only does this way of dealing with the matter deny the right to strike, but it puts the right to resort to arbitration in what seems to me to be an unreal position. I always thought that any two parties which have respect for each other and are on any kind of equal terms have a natural right at any time to agree to arbitrate and to agree to a third party sitting with them to ajudicate on a dispute; that they have the right in advance to agree, if they wish that arbitration will be accepted.
I suggest that the extent to which arbitration under this legislation becomes something that a bargaining unit has to choose three years in advance as an alternative to the right to strike, puts our public servants in a strait-jacket that is not consistent with the publicity that has been given to the idea that
