I hope that when we go into committee we may have an opportunity to take a new look at this. I think the choice should not have to be made in advance. If the right to strike is granted, it should be there on an unconditional basis.
I shall now move to another area which I think is a limitation in this bill. I refer to the grievance procedures which are established in it. There is much to be said for those procedures that is good, but I see two limitations. On the one hand I think that the range of matters that can be the subject of grievance procedure is too narrow, and on the other hand I suggest that the machinery for handling grievances involves the kinds of delays that can be fatal to a satisfactory solution to the grievances that employees or bargaining units may bring forward. I hope therefore that we can take a good look at the grievance procedure and perhaps improve it with respect to the points that I have made.
Another point to which I should like to draw attention relates to the whole question of how bargaining units are to be chosen and established, but I wish to draw attention more particularly to the fact that there are clauses in the bill which seem to me to open the door to what in certain circles, is called raiding. We will go into these defects when we get into committee on the bill, but I urge that if my reading of the bill is correct, if there are sections that make it possible for this practice to take place, we should tighten it up and make these provisions more clear.
There are certain areas in the bill where it seems to me that there are inequalities between the two sides, namely employer and employees. For example, I find that there are various penalties that are provided for employees or for representatives of bargaining units, penalties that are mostly monetary, but I find no corresponding penalty on the other side of the fence. I know the argument will be made that the employer on the other side is the government; perhaps eventually the employer is the parliament of Canada.
It seems to me, however, that if errors are made or if there is a departure from the spirit and intent of the whole principle of collective bargaining on the part of the individuals who represent the employer, similar to departures which are possible on behalf of individuals who represent the employees, some disciplinary measures should be enforced to assure equality on the two sides of the picture.


Finally I would like to draw attention to the fact that in this bill something is carried over from the old Civil Service Act which will also be carried forward if the government has its way, in the new public service employment act, and that is what amounts to an outright prohibition of political activities on the part of civil servants. The hon. member for Carleton used the words "political" in his speech, but he was not talking about the kind of political activity to which I refer.

given them that praise, we then make them second class citizens by denying them, for example, the right to collective bargaining that is accorded to employees in private industry.

I know that since I came to the house in 1953, I have been asking that the civil servants be given the right to negotiate with governmental authorities about their working conditions and salaries. The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson) pointed out that it took a long time for the act to become a reality in Canada.

But the Conservative party, including the hon. member for Carleton, was dead against giving the employees the right to negotiate their working conditions.
I do not intend to speak for a long time. A committee will study that matter and I hope that we will be given the opportunity to discuss that bill clause by clause and to make the necessary changes. I agree with all those who spoke before me and said that the legislation is not perfect. As a matter of fact, it was prepared by human beings and, therefore, reflects all the imperfections of human nature. It is possible to improve it. I say that the Liberal party will not object to amendments being submitted to improve it.
It is impossible to predict beforehand what the arbitration board will be like. I know that there will be such a board and that the employees and the government will each have a representative on it and that both of them will agree to find a third member able to understand their needs, those of the government and those of the employees.
That is how an understanding can be reached. I hope that it will be possible to create an arbitration board which will really be conscious of its obligations, and that is how we will be able to eliminate patronage, as mentioned a little earlier by the hon. member for Carleton. But as you know patronage is dead. There was a little in the past with regard to hourly-paid employees, but it has completely disappeared. With the new attitude which prevails today, it cannot exist. There was a time when I recommended hundreds of people and the hon. member for Carleton did the same thing. They were accepted. The new attitude has changed all that; it is impossible to recommend anyone. Once in a while, maybe, a man will be hired to replace another one; but it does not happen regularly any more. At the present time, contracts are given out. That may be preferable for I admit money can thus be saved. We were somewhat surprised to lose that opportunity of giving a man a job from time to time.
I agree that patronage must disappear, for it cannot improve the situation in parliament. It was done away with in Quebec and things are looking up. I believe the same will apply here when it has completely disappeared. Even

though the Creditistes do not seem to want to admit it-they do not believe in anything- they will not believe it until they have placed their hands in the wounds; doubting Thomases that they are, they do not want to believe.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on the principle of the bill and indicate some of the difficulties which I see in it, but before doing so I want to make clear that the suggestions I make are not intended to take anything away from the fact that this bill is a milestone in Canadian civil service history and, if it is improved in some respects, it will be an even more shining milestone than it is now.
My first suggestion is that the bill shows a certain amount of fear about the way in which in practice it would work out, with the result it is far too detailed. Too many t's are crossed and too many i's are dotted. There is too little discretion left to the board, and too little room for applying changing conditions. Everything is codified in a way which is likely to cause a great deal of difficulty in the actual, practical working out of this kind of legislation.
It would have been much better had the bill contained fewer specifics, had the government been prepared to let it rest on certain general principles and put the details into regulations which can much more easily be changed on the recommendation of the board, or of some other body which is specified in the bill. In my opinion this is the major defect in the bill. It attempts to set out almost every conceivable detail. I speak with some years of experience in such matters and I say that in labour relations it is impossible to do that and carry out an effective, practical job.
The second major difficulty about the bill is that the Public Service Staff Relations Board has far too many functions in addition to the certification of bargaining agents. It is not only given the job of certifying the bargaining agents, which should be undertaken by an entirely impartial third party, but it also has duties in relation to conciliation-in relation to


the items which are to be placed in conciliation, because its chairman sets them out-and it also has duties in relation to the appointment of adjudication and the manner in which they are to work.
In other words, it is a super board and because it is given powers-on the one side the certification of bargaining units, and on the other the authority to guide all the labour relations through the course of bargaining, conciliation and so on-it has too varied a set of powers to avoid becoming rigid. It will be much more concerned with the details of labour relations processes than would an ordinary labour relations board charged with certifying bargaining agents.
The body charged with certifying bargaining agents ought to be limited to that job, and I for one cannot see why that job could not be entrusted to the existing Canada Labour Relations Board. However, if the government felt it wanted some special civil service body to do that job and make that kind of decision, it could have a separate board undertake it, even though it be a part-time outfit meeting only for the purpose of dealing with certification applications, which do not arise often.
I repeat that it is a bad principle to have the body which creates the bargaining units, and therefore is the body which creates the instrument through which labour rights are to be enjoyed, also act as the body which in effect controls day by day the exercise of those rights the body which creates the rights ought to be separate from the body which controls the day by day exercises of those rights by the parties which gain them. For the life of me I do not see why it was not possible to place those two functions in two separate bodies.
My third general comment, which I make with all the emphasis at my command, is that the bill commits a terrible error in defining a bargaining unit in a detailed way, in effect almost saying to the body which is to certify the bargaining agent precisely what the composition of a bargaining unit should be.
It has been found by every labour relations board in every jurisdiction in Canada, and indeed in every other jurisdiction where such bodies exist, that this is an imprudent thing to do; that the prudent thing is to define a bargaining unit in the widest sensible terms -not the widest possible terms-and then leave to the board which certifies the bargaining agent enough discretion to be able to
May 31, 1966

adjust its certification to the demands of the parties, to the wishes of the parties, and to the particular circumstances surrounding the facts of an application for certification. The proposed board does not have that discretion. It is limited to certain stated, statutory categories, out of which it cannot move. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this will be found by the board, by the government and by the Public Service Commission to be a confinement that will be most impractical and undesirable.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
The fourth comment I wish to make is that there is a further limitation on the process of collective bargaining which, to me, is disturbing; that is, the statute gives the employer specific rights which it says are exclusive to the employer. I do not so much object to this being done as I object to the fact that the clause which gives the employer those rights does not make them subject in any way to the collective agreement between the parties.
For many years this was the case with collective agreements. They contained a proviso that such and such should be the exclusive function of management. But any modern collective agreement will provide that such and such shall be the exclusive function of management "subject to the provisions of this agreement". In other words, if the parties can agree that something in relation to dismissal or promotion for example, can be done in some other way than the way set out in some regulation, or the way desired by the employer, then the right of the employer should be qualified by the agreement of the parties in the case of a collective agreement, or by the award of the arbitrator in the case of arbitration. The terms of the bill constitute in this respect a serious limitation on collective bargaining.
My next point has to do with another example of the excessive power which has been given to the board as defined. There are provisions which say, in effect, that if an adjudicator or a board of arbitration trying to adjudicate or reach a settlement of a grievance bumps up against what is called a point of law or of jurisdiction, the adjudicator or the board does not have authority to deal with it but must refer it to the Public Service Staff Relations Board for decision. In the meantime, the arbitration proceedings cease.
In other words, there is a grievance procedure, provision is made for arbitration, and an attempt is made to provide an expeditious
Public Service Collective Bargaining way of settling the matter. Then the adjudicator or the board come up against a point of law-or someone argues it is a point of law. Usually it is the employer who says that jurisdiction to deal with a particular case is lacking. The board then goes home and has to refer the matter to a super board for a decision on the point of law or jurisdiction before arbitration can proceed. Again, this seems to be an instance where one board is given far too much power. There is nothing in labour relations which sours collective bargaining so quickly as protracted delays in the settlement of grievances.
In the same way it seems to me to be objectionable in principle that when conciliation is set up as one of the choices under the act it is not the parties themselves who set out the issues the conciliator has to deal with. They may signify these issues to the board, but it is the chairman of the super board who sets out in writing the matters to be dealt with and gives them to the conciliation board to consider. I cannot see the reason for this unless the government is setting out to take away with one hand part of what it is giving with the other; unless it is fearful of the results of genuine collective bargaining and wishes to place limits upon it.
The parties should be able to determine these matters themselves and if, in the course of conciliation proceedings, they happen to think of something else rather than what they thought of earlier, they should have the right to change. Often in the course of negotiations one party starts out asking for a, b and c while the other wants d, e and f' Then somebody says: give us g and we will abandon a and b. Unless the legislation provides for flexibility to meet situations of this kind, the machinery will work less effectively than it ought to work-I suppose to say it would be unworkable would be to use too extreme a word.
Finally, perhaps the minister would explain to us why two things are necessary. First, why should it be necessary to wait for as long as two years after this machinery has been established before certification takes place. It is for this reason that important changes of terminology are proposed: a public service employment act instead of a Civil Service Act; a public service commission instead of a Civil Service Commission.

By the standards then prevailing, the Civil Service Act of that year was one of the most advanced measures of its kind in the world. By establishing the merit system in a clearcut manner, it provided a foundation for what has come to be recognized throughout the world as a great public service. The Civil Service Act has served this country well and I hope that steps will be taken to ensure that its fiftieth anniversary, the year after next, will be appropriately marked.
The government believes that the essence of the 1918 act has been carried forward into Bill C-181. The principle of appointment and promotion according to merit has been retained and, if anything, stated more explicitly than ever before. Provision for an independent commission has also been retained. Indeed it is hoped that in some respects the proposed measure would put the commission in a position of even greater independence than that which it now enjoys. Finally the security of the merit principle has always been linked to the authority of the commission to control appointments to and promotions within the service. No part of the bill now before the house would in any way limit or qualify that ultimate authority.
Under the proposed legislation, the merit principle of appointment and promotion would not only be retained; it would in fact be extended to large areas of public service employment to which it has never before applied as a matter of law. I am sure that such changes will be welcomed by all those who value the non-political character and traditions of the public service.
I believe that in the preparation of Bill C-181 great care has been taken to preserve the merit principle. Let me make it clear however, that if, after careful examination and study, hon. members have any doubts about this, the government will be prepared to consider seriously any changes that may be suggested to improve the relevant provisions. We are satisfied that without the merit principle both the public service and the people of Canada would be less well served than they now are.
It should be noted, Mr. Speaker, that under the proposed legislation, the Public Service Commission would be given discretion to vary its methods and procedures in order to meet with maximum effectiveness the needs of different departmental programs and the conditions prevailing in the labour market. A conscious effort has been made to ensure that in the independent commission there is a capacity to respond flexibly and intelligently to changing requirements and circumstances.
Among other things, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-181 would permit the Public Service Commission to delegate its powers of appointment and promotion to the deputy heads of departments and the chief executive officers of other agencies. As the public service grows in size and complexity and as its activities affect an increasing number of citizens in so many important areas of their daily lives, it becomes essential for public administrators to be given increased authority to meet the demands that are made upon them quickly, realistically and efficiently, without reference in every case to a central agency. Unless such authority is made available, public administration tends to lose touch with reality, to become simply a matter of rules and regulations. Unless such authority is made available, it becomes increasingly difficult to ensure that the public interest is properly served. Just as it is important to protect the merit principle, so it is necessary to keep in mind the advantages to be gained in terms of administrative efficiency and effectiveness by a sensible distribution of authority within the public service. It is for this reason that the proposed measures would give the commission the capacity to delegate its appointing

The nature of delegated authority should not be misconstrued. Authority that may be delegated may also be withdrawn. Delegated authority is authority held in trust. It presumes a commitment on the part of those who accept it to use it in accordance with such direction as may be given by the delegating authority. It provides for a desirable administrative separation of those who determine policy and prescribe standards and those who apply policies and standards in the day to day administration of the public business.
It should be noted, Mr. Speaker, that the delegation of authority in no way removes responsibility from those to whom it is assigned by law. Under the proposed measure the Public Service Commission might delegate authority but it would retain responsibility for its exercise. The commission would be in a position to establish the conditions and standards governing the use of delegated authority and to monitor the exercise of such authority by departmental officers. It would also have the capacity to revoke an appointment made contrary to law or to the terms of delegation. Finally the commission would retain its traditional responsibility for the hearing and determination of appeals.
By making it possible for the commission to reduce its operational load, the proposed legislation would permit it to devote more attention to the development and maintenance of sound selection standards. It would also permit it to provide departments and Treasury Board with substantial assistance in career planning and in the administration of programs designed to make more effective use of scarce personnel resources.
Although responsibility for the effective utilization of manpower will rest with Treasury Board, Bill C-181 gives to the commission an important role in the operation of interdepartmental training and development programs and in the provision of assistance to deputy heads in the training and development of employees within departments. These are not new responsibilities. For the past decade the Civil Service Commission has made a substantial contribution to the efficiency of the public service through its training and development programs. It is hoped, however, that in its new role the commission will be able to increase the scope of existing programs and relate its activities in these areas more directly to the emerging requirements of the service.

The tradition of this house, since 1918 at least, has been that public service problems are discussed objectively and devoid of political partisanship. To that tradition I intend to be true in what I shall say tonight.

With the increasing involvement of government in every aspect of the daily life of the individual, the public service must be composed, I submit, of the very best-not the second best but the very best-and ablest of our young Canadians recruited for service to their nation. Sir, it is a significant fact that since its reconstitution in 1918 the Civil Service Commission has been the guardian of the merit system, responsible for appointments and promotions, but responsible as well for classification, establishment, standards and grades. It has been responsible further for recommendations as to salary and wage levels.
In effect, it has had a threefold role. Now, let it be clearly understood by the house, the new Public Service Commission will be shorn of two of these three roles or functions. Classification and establishment becomes exclusively a Treasury Board function, intended to be delegated as a general rule to deputy heads. In the jargon of the day, if I may so describe it, these allegedly are managerial functions to be now determined at the managerial level. The protection of an independent commission has been removed and the classification or the grade of an individual is placed squarely under the responsibility and jurisdiction of a political board, the Treasury Board, and of deputy ministers who, however non-political they may be, report after all to ministers who cannot be described as non-political.
Let this house remember, sir, that classification can be just as important as a salary increase. In the civil service those of us from Ottawa know that there is an old practice known as "classification creeping", which means giving a boost to an employee by

The commission has heretofore been the guardian against abuse in this respect. Hereafter, however, the commission will be eliminated from this area and the only protection against political, partisan and bureaucratic influences at work in a department will be the vigilance of the collective bargaining agents under the companion public service staff relations bill. Will the bargaining agents be either powerful enough or vigilant enough to protect against abuses in classification and establishment? They have no direct authority. Can they wield an indirect club?

Deputy ministers vulnerable to political pressures, and Treasury Board, which has a most competent and dedicated staff with a leading public servant as its secretary, but which, after all consists wholly of partisan politicians, will be taking the final decision and will have responsibility in this sensitive area.
I wonder what would happen if the golden, persuasive powers of, shall we say, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) were exercised upon his under secretary to induce the latter to recommend that "dear old Bill" be reclassified from grade 3 to grade 5. We know, of course, that the present Secretary of State for External Affairs would never do it. In his present portfolio, and previously as minister of national health and welfare, his statesmanlike qualities have completely subdued any innate partisanship he may have, even though not all his departmental officials have recognized his political objectivity. I am not prepared to accept their amateur preaching as necessarily gospel. At this late hour of the evening, I confess I am getting a little tired of royal commissions general.
The third field in which the present Civil Service Commission has responsibility at the present time is pay determination. This is to be, hereafter, the subject of collective bargaining. I say nothing further at this time on that subject except to welcome most heartily the decision of the government to retain the functions of the Pay Research Bureau. The point I want to make abundantly clear is that the new Public Service Commission will be a body very different indeed in authority and in jurisdiction from the existing Civil Service Commission. One of the by-products of the trifurcation-this is a word that has come into popular use in this house lately-of civil service procedures, is that discipline and dismissals are dispersed to three separate bodies. I say that a simple inquiry or investigation by the very body appealed from is not an appeal at all. It is just a sop and a sham. The only way to assure justice is to establish appeal panels of impartial persons outside the commission itself.
Now, the principles established by the government for adjudication of grievances, which would include dismissal for misconduct or for breach of discipline, as I have said are much to be preferred to the inadequate procedures provided in this bill for appeals from dismissal for incompetence, which incidentally is no longer defined, or for appeals in closed competitions. I think these provisions of the bill must be greatly strengthened, and I will submit that Bill No. C-63 shows the correct approach. I believe as well that the time has arrived to allow, under proper safeguards, at least a limited right of appeal in open competitions. It is in this field that I receive more complaints than any other, and some measure of relief to satisfy the complaints of unsuccessful applicants appears to me to be desirable now.
The minister has mentioned what is one of the most significant features of the bill, that is the proposal to bring under the ordinary procedures of selection, appointment and promotion, the prevailing rates employees, ships crews and officers. Personally, I endorse this proposal fully, and what I hope will be the complete abandonment of political patronage in this field. For many years I have been convinced that the continuation of patronage in the field of the trades and of ordinary labour is a blot upon our public personnel administration. I am sure that not all of our colleagues on either side of this house share that view. I do not profess to speak for colleagues on my own side in this respect. There are members on both sides of the house who look upon the existence and continuation of oatronage in the prevailing rates field as the bedrock of political organization. They take the attitude which one J. H. Price did in a letter to Robert Baldwin back on February 6, 1943, and I quote:
Patronage is power; our men won the victory, and they are entitled to prize money.
Business of the House
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
Well, sir, after having been responsible for probably as many patronage appointments as any other member present in this house, I am inclined to believe that patronage for a politician is a snare and a delusion. In my previous term I saw over 16,000 people from the Ottawa area seeking patronage employment, and I tell you that takes some doing. I think probably only the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) has ever equalled that. Few of us in this chamber have any training in personnel recruitment or management and I doubt whether the test of a good member of parliament should be his ability in this field. Personally, I welcome the new legislative proposal.
But I would give this warning: The techniques of examination and selection for the prevailing rates groups must not be too rigid or inflexible. It is unlikely they can be modelled upon the existing civil service examination procedure. Humanity and compassion must not be removed from the process of selection applicable to this type of employee. Some of the best prevailing rates employees today could never have passed any type of conventional examination. Among widows, long removed from the labour market, among those who have suffered major illnesses or other reverses in life, there will be found many wonderful people with the will and the incentive to succeed in this type of employment and I believe it is imperative that they should not be eliminated by standard tests or examinations designed for the youngsters just out of school.
Yes, wisdom, compassion and humanity must play a full part in the selection process. These were among the factors which politicians brought to their recommendations and they are factors which I believe must be continued in the new selection process.
But perhaps for the sake of compassion, wisdom and humanity I should call it ten o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, several times, but in vain, I have asked the incumbent Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) or her predecessors to put an end to the injustice being suffered by the people of Chibougamau and Chapais concerning television service.
I am told, as the taxpayers of those two cities are told, that the funds voted to the C.B.C. for service extension are inadequate and that they will have to wait.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am informed that the Northern Quebec Telephone Company Ltd. which has a microwave service between Grand Remous, Val d'Or, Rouyn and Chibougamau via Senneterre, and between Chibougamau and Notre Dame de la Dore, in Lake St. John, has offered its facilities to the C.B.C. to carry the television signal to Chibougamau-Chapais via Rouyn or Lake St. John.
That is why on May 20 last I asked the Secretary of State whether this offer had been considered and whether a decision had been taken on this matter. I know that the people of Chibougamau-Chapais are anxious to know what the intentions of the government are as regards this new possibility.
I believe that it would now cost little to the C.B.C. to use private enterprise, to co-operate with it to ensure a long-sought and wanted service to the people of Chibougamau-Chapais, a service to which they are entitled.
The Secretary of State has no more excuses and I hope that the citizens of Chibougamau-Chapais will be satisfied with the answer she will give tonight and I must point out that the only satisfactory answer will be the assurance that they will soon have the benefit of free television service, as is the case elsewhere in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I hope I can give satisfaction, on behalf of the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) and of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, to the population of Chibougamau-Chapais. Personally, I was ready a month ago to give the same answer to the hon. member, who had put the question last March.
The question of the hon. member, Mr. Speaker, raises this whole issue of the extension of television services in Canada.
Although no country in the world, except our United States neighbours, has more television and radio broadcasting stations, on the basis of population, than Canada, there are unfortunately-and the Secretary of State as well as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation realize this and work closely on this

remote areas which are not yet served or are inadequately served by this excellent education medium, that is television. One of these areas is that which interests the hon. member for Chapleau, namely Chibougamau-Chapais.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday, May 24, as
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion recorded in Hansard at page 5424, I put this question to the Prime Minister:
In view ol the statement made on Friday night-
The reference was to Friday night, May 20.
-in an address by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, to the effect that in Canada we are getting closer to the abolition of tuition fees in universities, will the Prime Minister say what steps the government is taking in this direction?
As Your Honour will recall, there were a number of questions on education that day and with your usual impartiality you treated all of them alike, and so this one got posted for the first available adjournment motion, namely tonight.
My question was based on a speech made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen), the text of which he was good enough to make available to us. But I also noticed a very good report of his speech in the Montreal Star of May 21, and I should like to quote two or three portions from the report in the Montreal Star:
The day "is not far off" when federal and provincial government officials will have to discuss with Canada's universities the abolition of tuition fees, health minister MacEachen said last night.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
Later on in the report I note this:
This being so, can we continue providing free education in that segment of the educational system which only lays the basic foundation for a space-age career, while maintaining the financial barriers in the higher education levels from which an increasingly greater percentage of our work force must come?
Then later these words:
Education is a responsibility of the provinces, Mr. MacEachen said. But the Federal Government had a responsibility to see that the "privilege" of higher education is transformed into "a right."
That indeed was a significant statement made by the minister with which I am sure all of us agree. He went on:
With the co-operation and understanding of all concerned, I think it will be possible for the Federal Government to fulfil its national obligations without eroding provincial prerogatives and without transgressing on academic freedom.
Mr. Speaker, I enjoyed reading the speech and I was pleased to see it so well reported in the Montreal Star. The sentiments were noble. What is the federal government doing about them?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with some bewilderment to the statement of the hon. member for Winnipeg North
May 31, 1966

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Centre (Mr. Knowles). He was asking a question of the Prime Minister concerning a statement made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I listened with interest to the statement, as reported by the hon. member, but I did not see with much clarity in what way the minister intended to exercise this federal government's intention, as expressed by him.
We all know that education primarily is the responsibility of the provinces. I should say that is is totally the responsibility of the provinces, except in very limited cases concerning protection of certain minority rights. I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is perfectly right in asking this kind of a question. Personally I should like to see him ask it of the minister who made the statement rather than of the Prime Minister.
I am in total agreement with the people who feel that a technological society such as we have in Canada should lend great importance to the area of education, and certainly the state should want to see that education becomes as universal as possible. The state, however, in this circumstance is the provincial state. The federal government, by way of bursaries and other aids to individuals, certainly can help the educational process; but stated in the way the hon. member asked the question, in other words in the way of acting towards the abolition of fees, this certainly is not a matter which is within federal jurisdiction. The federal government cannot in any way legislate toward the abolition of fees.

HEALTH AND WELFARE-GRANTS FOR RECREATION CENTRES FOR SENIOR CITIZENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday, May 27, I asked the following question:
Can consideration be given by the Department of National Health and Welfare to recommending grants for the construction of social and recreational centres for senior citizens equal In amount to grants by any province under an act of the legislature for such purpose?
The reason I asked this question was that at the present time the senior citizens club at Brantford, Ontario, is starting out on a campaign to raise funds to build a social and recreational centre for senior citizens of Brantford. The land has already been purchased. It is a very desirable piece of property, located very close to the centre of the municipality of the city of Brantford. I believe the club should be congratulated on the site it has chosen for this centre.
It is hoped that a start will be made on the building for the new social and recreational centre very shortly. An architect has been employed, the plans have been drawn for the new centre, and there is no doubt that a building of this kind is greatly to be desired and would be an excellent thing for all senior citizens of Brantford and vicinity who would desire to make use of such a centre.
For the information of the house I would point out that I have been in contact with various officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare and have been told that there is no basis for making a grant of this nature for the construction of a social and recreational centre for senior citizens. I can scarcely believe this to be true. However, Mr. Speaker, I do know that the federal government is being asked for grants for all sorts of beneficial projects from one end of Canada to the other and it is very difficult to start allocating money in this way.
At the same time I should like to point out that the municipality of the city of Brantford has agreed to pay 20 per cent of the cost of construction of this building and the province of Ontario has agreed to pay 30 per cent of the cost of construction. All I am asking is that the federal government agree to pay 30 per cent of such cost in order to match the provincial grant. The provincial grant is made possible under the elderly persons social and recreational centres act of Ontario, 1961-62 revised statutes of Ontario, chapter
May 31. 1966	COMMONS
37. Under this act the province of Ontario, as I have said, has agreed to pay 30 per cent of the cost. Under the act the province will not make this grant unless the municipality has agreed to pay 20 per cent of the cost. This has been done, and it becomes a question of whether the federal government will see fit to make a grant in this regard.
I know that such a centre would benefit large numbers of senior citizens in my constituency. It would be for their general health and well-being, and there is nothing I would like to see happen more than a contribution made by the federal government. I am sure the senior citizens of my constituency would benefit substantially by such a grant.
